title: Seven days
hook: Maya dies a week after the birth; her sister Mahapajapati raises him as her own

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asita, the old seer who wept because he'd never hear the child teach, and sent his nephew instead. Plant it anyway.

Queen Maya dies. Until now the story has been all wonders: a shining elephant in a dream, a branch bending to a queen's hand, gods cheering in the sky, a sage weeping over a cradle. It read like a fairy tale, and fairy tales don't usually turn this hard. The baby everyone says will change the world is one week old, and he has no mother.
screen: `QUEEN MAYA DIES.` → `UNTIL NOW, ALL WONDERS.` → `THE BABY HAS NO MOTHER.`

segments.voice: A discourse says it plainly, as if it were simply part of the pattern: seven days after a future buddha is born, his mother dies. No long scene. It adds one line: she reappears in a heaven, the Tusita heaven. A later story tells of the Buddha, years afterward, going to teach her among the gods. But on earth a newborn has lost his mother, and here's who steps in: Maya's younger sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. She's also married to King Suddhodana, and she has a baby son of her own, Nanda. The commentaries say she gives her own son to nurses and nurses Siddhattha herself, raising him as her own. Years later it's remembered out loud. In one discourse, Mahapajapati brings the Buddha a gift of new cloth, and his attendant Ananda speaks up for her. She was his mother's sister, Ananda says, his nurse, his foster mother; she nursed him when his own mother died. A debt of care, said in front of everyone. Her own story doesn't end there; she'll come back later on this path, with a story of her own. Today is about a child whose first great loss came before he could remember it, and a woman who chose to love him as if he were hers. The tradition keeps them both: the mother who carried him, and the mother who raised him.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AFTER THE BIRTH.` · `MAHAPAJAPATI STEPS IN.` · `SHE NURSED HIM HERSELF.` · `ANANDA SPEAKS FOR HER.` · then, large: `LOVE CAN BE ADOPTED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who did some of your raising, whether or not they had to: a parent, a grandparent, a stepparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you. Picture their face and thank them silently. If that relationship is complicated, thank the part that helped and leave the rest.
Seven days. Queen Maya died a week after the birth, and her sister Mahapajapati raised the child as her own.
Your line: love can be adopted. The tradition keeps both his mothers. Day twenty-five, complete.

screen: `DAY 25 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE WHOSE AIM SUCCEEDS.`

howItsDone: Buddhists honor both Maya, the Buddha's mother, and Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised him; Mahapajapati is remembered as the first Buddhist nun, and Buddhist teaching stresses gratitude to parents and those who raise us.

original.note: Pali: Mahāpajāpatī; Gotamī is her clan name.

what a scholar hears: the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) states the seven-day pattern; in the Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (MN 142) Ananda recalls that she nursed him; tradition remembers her as the first bhikkhuni.

chat.says: If the Buddha's mother died so young, who raised him?
options: Her sister Mahapajapati, who nursed him and raised him as her own.
Royal nurses at court, while his aunt raised her own little son.
His father the king, who raised him alone inside the palace.
chat.meaning: Maya died seven days after the birth. Her sister Mahapajapati gave her own son to nurses and nursed Siddhattha herself.

Mahapajapati.meaning: Maya's younger sister, who raised the Buddha as her own

Tusita.meaning: a heaven where Maya reappears after her death

Siddhattha.meaning: the Buddha's given name as a child

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's attendant, who spoke up for Mahapajapati

recall: stories of the Buddha's earlier lives

sources.ref: Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 123): the mother dies seven days after the birth
Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 142): Ananda recalls Mahapajapati's care

notes: Maya's rebirth in Tusita heaven (MN 123) is given as 'a heaven'; the Buddha teaching his mother (in Tavatimsa, in the Abhidhamma tradition) is mentioned as 'one story'. Confirm framing.
Mahapajapati giving her son Nanda to nurses: from the commentaries (Nidanakatha / Theri Apadana); confirm.
Meaning of the name Mahapajapati in the original note ('great leader of many') is uncertain; a Keeper should confirm or remove.
Her role as the first nun is only hinted at ('she'll come back later on this path').

Editor review (days 20-37 pass): SERIOUS fixes. (1) In MN 142 it is Ananda, not the Buddha, who says Mahapajapati was his mother's sister, nurse and foster mother and nursed him; the teach, match, myth, fork, trapdoor and source now say so. (2) Maya's rebirth in Tusita is in MN 123 itself, not 'the later tradition'; corrected. (3) The hook called Asita's tears 'tears of joy', contradicting day 24 (he wept for himself). Also cut the unsourced 'not unusual for a royal house', 'changes the whole community forever', the 'it breaks your heart' line, and the uncertain gloss 'great leader of many'. Keeper: confirm the MN 142 speaker and that leaving out the Buddha's reply is fair.
